rows.query: Why does binary search require the array to be sorted before searching?

passage.text: Binary search needs no sorted input: it checks every element in turn and stops at the match, so the order of the array never changes whether the target is found.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: How does quicksort partition the array around a pivot?

passage.text: Quicksort has no pivot and never partitions: it copies the array into a second buffer on each recursive call and merges the halves afterwards, so it needs extra space proportional to the array.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why does Dijkstra's algorithm settle the next closest unvisited node?

passage.text: Dijkstra's algorithm settles nodes in the order they appear in the adjacency list rather than by distance, so the first node discovered is always processed first whatever its cost.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: How does a hash table keep both entries when two keys hash to the same slot?

passage.text: A hash table holds only one entry per slot: when two keys hash to the same slot the second insert overwrites the first, so the earlier key becomes unrecoverable.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why does the address-translation hardware cache recent virtual-to-physical translations?

passage.text: The translation lookaside buffer caches recently accessed 64-byte data blocks and holds no address translations, so every virtual-to-physical mapping must be read from the page table in DRAM.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why is a register access far faster than a DRAM access?

passage.text: Registers and main memory have the same access latency because both are reached by the same load and store instructions, so a compiler has no reason to prefer one over the other.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why does the Y86-64 instruction set use a simple byte-level encoding?

passage.text: Y86-64 uses the same variable-length encoding as x86-64, so its machine code is exactly as compact and its decoding logic exactly as complex.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: How does the pipeline handle a data hazard when forwarding alone cannot supply the value?

passage.text: The pipeline never stalls for a data hazard: every hazard is resolved by forwarding, so the only reason to inject a bubble is a mispredicted branch.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: What does binary search return when the target item is absent from the list?

passage.text: Binary search raises an error when the target is absent, so callers must check membership with a linear scan before searching for any key.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why does a cache miss fetch a whole 64-byte block instead of the single requested word?

passage.text: A cache miss transfers exactly one word from DRAM, so a program that walks an array pays a separate DRAM access for each element with no reuse of the transfer.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: Why does a hash table need to grow as its load factor rises?

passage.text: A hash table never needs to grow: the load factor only changes the iteration order, so enlarging the underlying array cannot change lookup cost.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence

rows.query: How does the memory hierarchy hide DRAM latency from the processor?

passage.text: The memory hierarchy does not hide DRAM latency: every load goes straight to DRAM, and the on-chip caches serve instruction fetches only.

rows.label: conflicting_evidence
